idiom_name: abstract record base with a private constructor + sealed nested records + switch expression
implementation_notes: The C#-native approximation is a closed hierarchy built from records: an abstract record base whose private constructor only the nested, sealed variant records can call, so no shape outside the file can be added. Positional records give each state its own payload and value equality, and a switch expression with type patterns consumes the set. What replaces the sealed structure is that private base constructor plus nested sealed records - C# has no compiler-checked closed-set or exhaustive union before C# 15, so a switch that misses a variant compiles with warning CS8509 unless warnings are errors; the type still guarantees the legal shapes, and the missing-arm warning is the compiler's closest approximation of exhaustiveness. Keep the hierarchy in one file and treat adding a variant as a breaking change.
pitfalls: A switch expression over the hierarchy is not proven exhaustive (warning CS8509, not an error): leave the discard arm out and fail the build on warnings, or a new variant is handled nowhere.
The private base constructor has to be repeated in every nested record's declaration scope - moving a variant to another file breaks the closure, so keep the hierarchy in one file.

System.Text.Json serializes records with a type discriminator only if the base is declared with [JsonDerivedType] - otherwise deserializing the base type loses the variant and re-opens the illegal state.

variants.name: C# 15 union types with compiler-checked exhaustive matching
variants.idiom_name: union keyword over fresh case records
variants.implementation_notes: C# 15 adds the union keyword: a value is exactly one of a fixed set of case types and the compiler knows the set, so switch expressions over a union are exhaustiveness-checked and adding a case type produces warnings at every switch that does not handle it. Declare fresh record types for the cases (a discriminated union is expressed as a type union over freshly declared case types) and use pattern matching directly on the union value - it unwraps to the underlying case. Prefer this variant once the toolchain is on C# 15, because it restores the compile-time exhaustiveness that the record-hierarchy variant can only approximate; the library-provided union types of earlier years stay useful only for codebases pinned to older compilers.
pitfalls: The generated union struct has a null state (Value can be null), so a switch over a union that is maybe-null still needs a null arm - nullability analysis is separate from case exhaustiveness.
Union values box value-type cases: a union of structs allocates, so for hot paths use the non-boxing access pattern (HasValue plus TryGetValue) on a custom union instead of the generated struct.
The compiler warns rather than errors on a missed case unless the project treats warnings as errors; the union does not make the missing arm impossible, only visible.
